name: The Wild Hunt
description: The ghostly host of riders and hounds that storms across the winter sky, bringing trouble to anyone who sees it
origin: Folklore of northern and western Europe

debut.title: European folk tradition
debut.era: recorded in England in the 12th century, and named by Jacob Grimm in 1835

legend: On stormy winter nights, a host of spectral riders is said to sweep across the sky with horns blowing and hounds baying. Who leads it depends on where you are standing. In Scandinavia it is Odin, and the Norwegians call the host the Oskoreia. In German lands it is the Wilde Jagd, sometimes led by a woman such as Frau Perchta. In Britain the leaders include King Herla, who in Walter Map's 12th-century telling can never dismount. The Peterborough Chronicle's entry for 1127 describes black huntsmen riding black horses and black goats, with black hounds. In many tellings the Hunt rides in the long nights around midwinter and the Twelve Days of Christmas, and to see it was widely held to foretell war, plague or a death.

myths.claim: The Wild Hunt is always led by Odin.
myths.explanation: Only in Scandinavia. Elsewhere its leaders include King Herla, Frau Perchta and many others.

myths.claim: It only ever rides at Christmas.
myths.explanation: Midwinter is its usual season, but not its only one: the Peterborough chronicler's huntsmen were seen in late winter and into spring.

myths.claim: Jacob Grimm gave it its best-known name.
myths.explanation: He wrote about the Wilde Jagd in his Deutsche Mythologie of 1835, and the name stuck.

myths.claim: Seeing it was thought to be a bad omen.
myths.explanation: It was widely held to foretell war or plague, or the death of whoever saw it.

weaknesses: Anyone sensible enough to stay indoors
legacy: Peter Nicolai Arbo's painting Åsgårdsreien (1872), now in Norway's national museum
Jacob Grimm's Deutsche Mythologie (1835), which made it a subject for scholars
